name: Bhutan
genZNote: Bhutan looked at GDP and said 'no thanks' — it measures itself in Gross National Happiness instead, and its constitution literally mandates keeping 60% of the country under forest cover, forever.

sections.heading: 🗺️ Geography
bullets: A small, landlocked Himalayan kingdom in South Asia, sandwiched between India to the south, east, and west, and China (Tibet Autonomous Region) to the north.
Entirely mountainous terrain, ranging from subtropical plains in the south to high Himalayan peaks (including Gangkhar Puensum, one of the world's highest unclimbed mountains) in the north.
The world's only carbon-negative country — its forests absorb more carbon than the nation emits — and the Constitution requires at least 60% forest cover to be maintained at all times.

sections.heading: 🗣️ People & Culture
bullets: Dzongkha is the national language; Vajrayana Buddhism is the dominant religion and shapes daily life, architecture, and festivals.
Famous for prioritising Gross National Happiness (GNH) over GDP as a guiding development philosophy, formalised into government policy since the 1970s.
Distinctive fortress-monasteries called dzongs serve as both administrative and religious centres in every district.
National dress — the gho for men and kira for women — is required in schools, government offices, and formal settings.

sections.heading: 🏛️ Government & Society
bullets: A constitutional monarchy since 2008, when King Jigme Singye Wangchuck voluntarily transferred power from an absolute to a constitutional monarchy — a rare case of a monarch initiating his own reduction in power.
The King (Druk Gyalpo, 'Dragon King') is head of state; a bicameral Parliament (National Assembly and National Council) and an elected government handle day-to-day governance.
Divided into 20 dzongkhags (districts), each administered around its historic dzong.

sections.heading: 🧬 Medical & Scientific Developments
bullets: Healthcare and education are constitutionally guaranteed as free public services, reflecting the GNH policy framework.
A recognised model in environmental and conservation science, with strict logging limits and a national commitment to remaining carbon-negative.
Hydropower engineering is the country's main technical/scientific sector, with river-fed plants supplying both domestic power and export electricity to India.

sections.heading: 🌐 Global Relations
bullets: Member of the United Nations, SAARC, and BIMSTEC.

Notably does not maintain formal diplomatic relations with any of the five permanent UN Security Council members (China, France, Russia, UK, USA) — one of very few countries in this position — and has diplomatic ties with a comparatively small number of nations overall.
Foreign and defence policy has historically been closely coordinated with India under the Bhutan-India Friendship Treaty.

sections.heading: 🇮🇳 Relations with India
bullets: India and Bhutan share a uniquely close 'special relationship', formalised by the Treaty of Friendship (1949, revised 2007), with India as Bhutan's largest development partner and trading partner by far.
India funds and assists major Bhutanese hydropower projects, and imports the resulting electricity — a cornerstone of the bilateral economic relationship.
The Bhutanese Ngultrum is pegged 1:1 to the Indian Rupee, and the Rupee is widely accepted within Bhutan.
The 2017 Doklam standoff, near the India-Bhutan-China tri-junction, underscored India's strategic role in supporting Bhutan's territorial interests.

sections.heading: 📦 Trade & Economy
bullets: Hydropower exports to India are the backbone of the economy, alongside agriculture, forestry, and a small but growing tourism sector.
Tourism follows a deliberate 'high value, low volume' policy: visitors pay a Sustainable Development Fee, keeping numbers controlled rather than maximised.
As a small, landlocked economy, Bhutan depends heavily on India for trade routes, imports, and market access.

sections.heading: ⭐ What It's Known For
bullets: Gross National Happiness as a national development philosophy, in place of GDP-only growth metrics.
Being the world's only carbon-negative country, with constitutionally protected forest cover.
Paro Taktsang (the 'Tiger's Nest' monastery), built into a cliffside above the Paro valley.
A tightly managed, high-value tourism model rather than mass tourism.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Bhutan is a small, landlocked Himalayan constitutional monarchy between India and China, known for prioritising Gross National Happiness and remaining carbon-negative.
keyFacts: Capital: Thimphu. Currency: Ngultrum (pegged 1:1 to the Indian Rupee).
Became a constitutional monarchy in 2008, transitioning voluntarily from absolute monarchy.
Constitution mandates a minimum of 60% forest cover.
No formal diplomatic relations with any UNSC permanent member.
commonConfusion: Bhutan is a CONSTITUTIONAL monarchy since 2008, not an absolute one — the shift was voluntary, initiated by the King himself, not forced by revolution.

highYieldFacts: Bhutan: only carbon-negative country in the world; 60% forest cover is a constitutional requirement.
Constitutional monarchy since 2008; capital Thimphu; currency Ngultrum pegged to INR.
Bhutan-India Treaty of Friendship: signed 1949, revised 2007.
commonTraps: Assuming Bhutan uses GDP as its primary development metric — it deliberately emphasises Gross National Happiness instead.
Confusing Bhutan's currency (Ngultrum) with India's Rupee — they are pegged 1:1, but are distinct currencies.
mustRemember: Bhutan: Himalayan constitutional monarchy, GNH philosophy, carbon-negative, hydropower-dependent economy tightly linked to India.
